primer.title: Owned, borrowed, and keyed
body: `String` owns its text on the heap; `&str` is a borrowed view of text that lives somewhere else. A `&String` coerces to `&str` automatically, but a `String` passed *by value* does not.
`iter()` lends out `&T`, `iter_mut()` lends out `&mut T` (write through it with `*n`), and `into_iter()` on a `Vec` gives away each `T`.
`map.entry(key).or_insert(v)` inserts `v` only if the key is absent, and returns `&mut` to the value either way:

exercises.prompt: This does not compile. What does the compiler object to?
code: println!("That is a color word I know!");
println!("That is not a color word I know.");

options.text: E0308: line 8 passes a `String` where `&str` is expected
options.rationale: Rust never borrows for you at a call site. `&word` would work: `&String` coerces to `&str`.
A move would be legal here — `word` is not used afterwards. The call is rejected earlier, on its types.
`&str == &str` compares the text and is used all the time.
Lifetimes in parameters are elided. Annotations are only needed when a *returned* reference is ambiguous.
`trim` returns a sub-slice, `to_uppercase` and `replace` return new `String`s. None of them changes the value it is called on.
`replace` does not modify `shout`; it returns a new `String`, bound to `swapped`.
`trimmed` is the slice that `trim` returned, without the surrounding spaces.
`to_uppercase` builds a new `String`; `trimmed` still points into the original lowercase text.
`iter().map()` builds a new vector and only reads `input`. `iter_mut()` changes `tripled` in place — but that is a clone.
`map` never modifies its source; `input` is not even `mut`.

options.text: It does not compile: `input` was moved by `iter()`
options.rationale: `iter()` only borrows. It is `into_iter()` that would consume the vector.
`or_insert` leaves existing keys alone, so only banana gets 5. Apple becomes 4 + 1: 5 + 5 + 2 = 12.
This assumes `or_insert(5)` overwrote apple and mango. It only inserts when the key is missing.
Line 11 adds 1 to apple: `or_insert` returns `&mut` to the existing value, and `*… += 1` writes through it.
A map holds each key once. `entry` on an existing key does not add a second one.
